title: By My Life, I Have Never Made a Habit of Mourning the Dead
intro: Mutammim ibn Nuwayra mourns his brother Malik, killed in the wars following the Prophet’s death. Al-Yazidi relates that al-Minhal found the fallen man and covered him with his cloak. Mutammim remembers how Malik used to feed others and stand by them, asks rain to visit his grave, and answers a woman who wants to know what has changed him. The cries of three camels over one lost calf bring him back to the man who hurried off to announce Malik’s death.

translation: By my life, I have never made a habit of mourning the dead
or of losing heart at a blow that hurts.
1.sharh: “My time” is how he speaks of the practice of his whole life. He begins an elegy by telling us what an exceptional thing it is for him to utter one.

translation: Under his own cloak al-Minhal shrouded
a striking young man who never gorged himself at supper.
2.sharh: Malik first appears as a body covered by another man. The measure of his life is taken at the evening meal, when keeping food for oneself might leave a guest hungry.

translation: No man to sit out the stakes while women sent his wife food
when winter cold made the hide shelter crackle.
3.sharh: In winter the men took on the price of a slaughter camel and drew lots for its meat. A household that always received and never took the risk would be remembered for it.

translation: A discerning man, his judgement helped by open-handedness,
a land of plenty when the famine-rider hurried on.
4.sharh: Wisdom and generosity assist one another in him. The hungry traveller is still on the move when the poet calls the man he is heading for a stretch of fertile ground.

translation: You saw him quiver like the forward part of a sword, eager to give,
when no hope of a gift remained at a mean man’s door.
5.sharh: The sword is a measure of responsiveness. His quickness shows most clearly when the same request has failed to stir anybody else.

translation: On a day when an adversary pressed you hard, if he stood
as your champion among them, yours was no lost cause.
6.sharh: The second person places a listener inside the dispute. The pressure of many opponents changes as soon as one man takes up the listener’s claim.

translation: Meeting him among the drinkers, you found no foul mouth
at the cup, no ill-tempered brawler.
7.sharh: Companions at a drinking party see a man when his guard is down. The double description covers both what he might say and the quarrel he might start.

translation: When raiding had sunk its teeth into men, you saw
a true brother of battle, a chief who stood his ground.
8.sharh: Raiding is made into a creature with teeth. “Brother of war” suggests a long familiarity that proves itself when battle begins to hurt.

translation: He never hung back when the horses balked,
nor rushed in heedlessly to be thrust aside.
9.sharh: Cavalry wheeling back supplies one test of nerve. Being able to go forward without losing control supplies the other.

translation: Nor was his equipment blunt against a foe,
whether he faced him bareheaded or helmeted.
10.sharh: The Arabic gives the man’s whole equipment the quality of a dulled edge and denies that it ever had it. He was equal to an opponent in either state of preparedness.

translation: My two eyes, will you not weep for Malik
when the wind scatters the shelter that stood so high?
11.sharh: A windbreak coming apart creates an immediate need for shelter. His brother’s absence can now be felt by anyone standing out in the cold.

translation: Weep for Malik at the drinking circle, and for the champion
so formidable on every side to anyone playing the brave.
12.sharh: There is an empty place at the gathering and another when a champion must step forward. The hard-to-approach fighter is seen from the position of the man who would take him on.

translation: And for the guest whose camel groans at a night arrival,
and the captive kept in rawhide till his limbs stiffen.
13.sharh: The traveller announces himself by the noise of his mount. The prisoner makes no such entrance, so the length of his confinement has to be read in his limbs.

translation: And the widow walking with an unkempt, underfed child,
his hair sticking out like the down of a bustard chick.
14.sharh: The widow does not have to voice an appeal. The ungroomed head and poor growth of the child walking with her make the household’s need visible.

translation: When men drew the gaming arrows bare and lit
the players’ fire, he covered for anyone hanging back.
15.sharh: The arrows and the fire launch a public distribution of meat. Malik’s part begins before there is anything to give away, when someone has to guarantee the expense.

translation: And when he joined the players you never found Malik
over the paunch, guarding the meat against division.
16.sharh: The paunch locates the scene beside the freshly killed animal. A man who took the largest risk might press the hardest claim, but nobody finds Malik standing guard there.

translation: Things I see refuse me patience, and I
see every bond since yours cut short.
17.sharh: Bonds are imagined as serviceable lengths of rope. He measures every attachment still available to him against the reach of the lost one.

translation: Whenever I call your name you do not answer.
You were always the one to hear and answer.
18.sharh: The Arabic changes from description of Malik to speech directed at him. A call that used to bring help now produces a silence the speaker can reproduce at will.

translation: We lived well together. Before our time
death struck the house of Kisra and struck Tubba'.
19.sharh: The two royal names take him far outside his own family. A Persian king’s household and a south Arabian ruler offer precedents even a powerful family has to accept.

translation: When at last we parted, Malik and I,
for all those years together, seemed never to have shared a night.
20.sharh: The long companionship and the single night are deliberate extremes. It is the parting, not a failure of memory, that makes so much shared time feel inaccessible.

translation: For ages we were like Jadhima’s two table companions,
until people said the pair would never be parted.
21.sharh: Jadhima’s inseparable companions were a proverbial pair. The brothers’ closeness was visible from outside the family too, as the otherwise unnamed people who spoke of it testify.

translation: If the days have come between us,
my brother went away acclaimed when he took his leave.
22.sharh: Time can settle the fact of separation. The word of leave-taking allows a final glimpse of Malik among people who still speak well of him.

translation: I speak as lightning flies through low scraps of cloud
and a dark cloud pours water till it brims and spills.
23.sharh: His words are held back for a verse while we watch the storm. A wish for water will follow from an actual sight of water in the sky.

translation: May God water the land that holds Malik’s grave
with the rains of overcast mornings and make it green.
24.sharh: Asking rain for a grave is an old form of greeting the dead. Here the landscape can respond to a wish although Malik could not respond to his name.

translation: May He favour the channels of the two valleys with steady rain
that brings up tender growth from the season’s first showers.
25.sharh: The opening flood needs a slower rain to sustain its work. The wish follows moisture beyond the watercourse into shoots tender enough to bend.

translation: And the meeting of the standing waters round Shari',
drenching the hills of al-Qaryatayn and then Dalfa'.
26.sharh: The place names give the blessing a route. The repeated Arabic connective moves water from one named piece of country to the next, almost without a pause.

translation: By God, no love of lands makes me call rain upon them.
I call it down for the loved one I laid to rest.
27.sharh: He has described the country so closely that he pauses to explain his motive. The change from many lands to one loved person gives the whole prayer its address.

translation: My greeting to him, however far away he is,
though he has turned to dust with barren earth above him.
28.sharh: The rain is a greeting the living can send across a distance. Immediately afterwards we are returned to the grave as he knows it, with bare ground overhead.

translation: Al-Amri’s daughter says, “What has happened to you? Only lately
I saw you carefree, with a fine head of hair.”
29.sharh: An observer brings the effects of mourning back to the body. She remembers the man as he looked a short while ago, which makes the present change startling.

translation: I told her when she asked, “Long sorrow,
and a burning grief that darkens a man’s face.”
30.sharh: The woman can see a change of colour before she knows its cause. His answer gives the burning of an inward grief a mark it can leave on skin.

translation: “And the loss of sons of one mother who followed each other.
With them gone, I could hardly cower and submit.”
31.sharh: “Called to one another” makes successive deaths sound like an exchange among brothers. The survivor has fewer people behind him and still feels answerable to them.

translation: I go on through it, stepping forward
when some who meet a battle start to back away.
32.sharh: He keeps his grief with him as he advances. The stuttering consonants of the last Arabic verb suit the steps of someone drawing back.

translation: What took Qays and Malik has changed me,
and Amr and Juz' at al-Mushaqqar, together.
33.sharh: The names accumulate faster than their histories can be told. The old explanations disagree about the men and the occasions of their deaths, especially about identifying this Malik with the brother.

translation: And what took Yazid, my drinking companion. I wish
I could have bought more time with him for all my kin and wealth.
34.sharh: Yazid gets a relation as well as a name. The wish puts family and possessions together on one side of a bargain whose only return would be more time with him.

translation: Though you trade jests with me, I have suffered
grief enough to make a stricken mourner weep.
35.sharh: A woman close enough to joke with him might take an easy answer as a sign of recovery. The speaker lets her see what remains after the exchange is over.

translation: When time brings some fresh blow upon me
and some loss, I do not creep from kinswoman to kinswoman.
36.sharh: The emphatic word for a habitual visitor matters. He distinguishes the conversation now taking place from making a round of the women of his family in search of pity.

translation: I beg you, spare me any reproach.
Do not pick my heart’s wound and set it aching.
37.sharh: The plea takes the form of an adjuration. A healing sore can be opened by touch, which is the precise harm her well-meant words could do.

translation: Enough. I was there, and I found
nothing in my hand that could keep death from them.
38.sharh: She has asked what changed him. He saw the people he loved die and looked in vain to his own hand for some means of saving them.

translation: I am not carried away by a day of good fortune
or undone by whatever has struck me and hurt.
39.sharh: The closing words repeat the opening. By now the listener knows exactly which experiences lie behind a claim that might once have sounded like indifference.

translation: If what I endure were to strike Mutali'
or a buttress of Salma, it would shake it loose.
40.sharh: A whole mountain and a supporting flank of another mountain supply two measures of resistance. The scale answers the restraint he claimed a moment ago.

translation: Think of the grief of three tender foster-camels
who find where their calf was dragged and where it fell.
41.sharh: All three have nursed the same calf, so the one set of tracks is a loss for every one of them. The sentence leaves their grief suspended until the fourth verse of the comparison.

translation: They remind a grieving man of his own sorrow
when the first moans and the others answer her together.
42.sharh: There are two audiences for the first cry, the other camels and the listening man. Grief travels between species as well as spreading through the herd.

translation: When one old she-camel rises and repeats her cry,
her grief sets the whole kneeling herd to weeping.
43.sharh: A single animal stands above all the others that are still on the ground. Her repeated call widens the scene beyond the three foster-mothers.

translation: Their grief was no greater than mine the day a man rose
to cry Malik’s death, knowing what parting meant, and made himself heard.
44.sharh: Only now does the comparison close. The chorus of bereaved animals leads back to one human voice and the instant the death became public knowledge.

translation: Has word of al-Muhill’s conduct failed to reach your chiefs,
to stir the anger of everyone among you who feels this loss?
45.sharh: He addresses the people who can call the witness to account. Hearing news of a death and hearing news of how someone behaved at that death are two different obligations.

translation: About his gloating when death found Malik,
about what he saw in person and then neglected.
46.sharh: Al-Muhill both rejoiced and failed to act. His own presence removes the excuse that he came too late to see what the fallen man needed.

translation: Did you choose an old rag and a saddle pad,
then come running with the news, a courier stripped for speed?
47.sharh: Even a worn wrapper or a cloth from the saddle could have covered the body. The messenger’s haste makes a pointed counterpart to al-Minhal stopping to spread his cloak.

translation: Never take such pleasure in yourself. I see
death come down hard on anyone who plays the hero.
48.sharh: The courier lived to tell the tale once. He is asked to consider how little that tells him about his own chances, especially if he makes a show of courage.

translation: One day a calamity may well come upon you,
one of those that leave a man with his nose cut off.
49.sharh: Mutilation would put a lasting mark on the very face with which the man showed his pleasure. The threat gives disgrace a visible form.

translation: You announced the death of a man who, given your flesh,
would have sheltered it, whole or torn to pieces.
50.sharh: The dead man is allowed the last act of generosity in the poem, through a reversal imagined by his brother. It is precisely the service the living witness failed to perform.

translation: May Malik’s killing bring the tale-bearers no joy.
The man who hated him went home and bade farewell in turn.
51.sharh: The last wish extends to everyone who carried hostile tales. The verb of leave-taking used for the beloved brother returns at the very end for his enemy.

1.1.3.head: دَهر
1.1.3.meaning: One’s settled habit, what one ordinarily spends a lifetime doing.

1.1.4.head: تَأبين
1.1.4.meaning: Commemorating a dead person by naming his good qualities.

2.1.3.head: المِنهال
2.1.3.meaning: Al-Minhal ibn Isma of Yarbu, who in al-Yazidi’s account spread his cloak over Malik’s body.

2.2.3-4.head: مِبطان العَشِيّات
2.2.3-4.meaning: “An evening glutton.” One who eats his fill, or makes himself scarce at supper so as to eat alone.

2.2.5.head: أَروَع
2.2.5.meaning: Striking in appearance and bearing, someone who commands attention.

3.1.2.head: بَرَم
3.1.2.meaning: A man who sits out the arrow game and relies on others to send meat.

3.1.5.head: عِرس
3.1.5.meaning: His wife, who would receive meat allotted to the household.

3.2.2.head: القَشع
3.2.2.meaning: Dry hide, or a shelter of hides that creaks in the cold.

3.2.4.head: بَرد
3.2.4.meaning: Winter cold, which makes the hide shelter rattle. Other witnesses give winter’s sting or winter’s wind.

4.2.4-5.head: راكِب الجَدب
4.2.4-5.meaning: “Rider of drought,” a traveller hastened on by famine.

4.2.6.head: أَوضَعَ
4.2.6.meaning: Urged a mount into a rapid gait.

5.2.5-6.head: اِمرُؤ السَّوء
5.2.5-6.meaning: A mean-spirited man who gives the petitioner no grounds for hope.

6.1.4.head: كَظَّ
6.1.4.meaning: Pressed you hard enough to leave you feeling stifled.

6.2.6.head: أَضيَع
6.2.6.meaning: Left without a defender, liable to lose one’s case or rights.

7.1.4.head: الشَّرب
7.1.4.meaning: A company of drinkers gathered together.

7.2.5.head: مُتَزَبِّع
7.2.5.meaning: A quarrelsome, ill-tempered member of the drinking party.

8.1.2.meaning: Bit as with molar teeth, here the hard schooling of war.

8.2.6.head: سَمَيدَع
8.2.6.meaning: A chief distinguished by courage and generosity.

9.1.6.head: أَحجَمَ
9.1.6.meaning: Balked or drew back from danger, here of the cavalry.

9.2.5.head: مُدَفَّع
9.2.5.meaning: Easily thrust aside or treated as of little account in battle.

10.1.2.head: كَهام
10.1.2.meaning: Blunt or ineffectual, originally of a blade that will not cut.

10.2.4.head: حاسِر
10.2.4.meaning: Bareheaded, having no helmet or covering of mail.

11.2.2.head: أَذرى
11.2.2.meaning: Lifted and scattered something, as a strong wind does.

11.2.4.head: الكَنيف
11.2.4.meaning: A raised shelter or windbreak for livestock.

12.1.4.head: بُهمَة
12.1.4.meaning: A champion whom no one knows how to overcome. The word can also name a formidable body of troops.

12.2.2.head: ناحِيَة
12.2.2.meaning: The approaches by which an opponent might try to reach the champion.

13.1.3.meaning: Made the camel call, to announce arrival or find the camp from the answering calls.

13.2.1.head: عانٍ
13.2.1.meaning: A prisoner held in bonds and in need of release.

13.2.4.head: القِدّ
13.2.4.meaning: A rawhide thong used for binding.

13.2.6.head: تَكَنَّعَ
13.2.6.meaning: Grew stiff and contracted from prolonged restraint.

14.2.5.head: تَضَوَّعَ
14.2.5.meaning: Spread out untidily, of hair or down. Al-Yazidi transmits a form with s instead of d.

15.1.4.head: قِدح
15.1.4.meaning: The marked arrows drawn to determine shares in a slaughter camel and liability for its price.

15.2.3.head: ياسِر
15.2.3.meaning: Participants in the arrow game over a camel to be divided as meat.

15.2.6.head: تَضَجَّعَ
15.2.6.meaning: Held back from taking a share of the expense.

16.2.2.head: الفَرث
16.2.2.meaning: The contents of the paunch, marking the spot where the animal has been dressed.

16.2.6.head: تَوَزَّعَ
16.2.6.meaning: Is shared out among the group. Al-Yazidi also records “be torn into pieces”, another way of picturing the division of the meat.

17.1.3.head: آيَة
17.1.3.meaning: Signs around him that call his brother back to mind.

17.2.3.head: حَبل
17.2.3.meaning: A bond joining two people, imagined as a rope one can hold.

19.2.4.meaning: Kisra, the Arabic title of the Sasanian rulers of Persia.

19.2.5.head: تُبَّع
19.2.5.meaning: Tubba', a title of the Himyarite kings in Yemen.

21.1.2-3.head: نَدمانا جَذيمَة
21.1.2-3.meaning: Jadhima’s two boon companions, identified by al-Yazidi as Malik and Aqil and proverbial for staying together.

21.2.6.head: تَصَدَّعَ
21.2.6.meaning: Come apart, as something whole splits.

23.1.4.meaning: The flash or radiance of lightning.

23.1.6.head: رَباب
23.1.6.meaning: Thin, low cloud hanging under the darker rain clouds.

23.2.1.head: جَون
23.2.1.meaning: A dark mass of rain cloud.

24.2.1.head: ذِهاب
24.2.1.meaning: Rainfalls, plural of dhihba, here showers brought by the morning clouds.

24.2.3.head: مُدجِنَة
24.2.3.meaning: Clouds that cover the sky and persist with rain.

25.1.4.head: ديمَة
25.1.4.meaning: A steady, sustained rain that soaks the ground.

25.2.2.head: وَسمِيّ
25.2.2.meaning: Growth raised by the early seasonal rain, which “marks” the soil with plants.

25.2.5.head: خِروَع
25.2.5.meaning: Supple young vegetation, readily bent. No particular species is required.

26.1.2.head: سَدَم
26.1.2.meaning: Standing waters grown stale or silted up over time.

26.1.5.head: شارِع
26.1.5.meaning: Shari', a place named on the route the poet wishes the rain to take.

26.2.3.head: القَريَتان
26.2.3.meaning: Al-Qaryatayn, the place whose surrounding hills the poet singles out for rain.

26.2.4.head: ضَلفَع
26.2.4.meaning: Dalfa', the last place named in the rain prayer.

27.1.3.head: أَسقى
27.1.3.meaning: Ask that a place be watered, a traditional blessing for land or grave.

29.1.2-3.head: اِبنَة العَمرِيّ
29.1.2-3.meaning: The daughter of al-Amri, named through her father when she speaks to the bereaved man.

29.2.5.head: أَفرَع
29.2.5.meaning: With a full head of hair, as the woman remembers him before his loss.

30.2.1.head: لَوعَة
30.2.1.meaning: A burning pang of grief. The texts give the singular. The sustained vowel can also sound like the plural, “pangs”.

30.2.5.head: أَسفَع
30.2.5.meaning: Darkened, with a reddish cast, a change grief leaves in the face.

31.1.4.head: تَداعى
31.1.4.meaning: “They called one another.” One brother followed another to his death.

31.2.1.head: خِلاف
31.2.1.meaning: After them, once the others are gone.

32.2.6.head: تَكَعكَعَ
32.2.6.meaning: Recoil or fall back in fear.

33.2.3.head: المُشَقَّر
33.2.3.meaning: Al-Mushaqqar, a stronghold in historical Bahrayn. Accounts differ on how the named men relate to fighting there.

33.2.4.meaning: An unusual form construed as “together” by one line of commentators. Another explanation connects it with disappearing.

34.1.3.head: نَدمان
34.1.3.meaning: My boon companion, a word earlier used of Jadhima’s pair of companions.

34.1.4.head: يَزيد
34.1.4.meaning: Yazid, the poet’s companion, described in a report preserved by al-Yazidi as his cousin.

34.2.1.head: تَمَلّى
34.2.1.meaning: Enjoyed someone’s company over a long stretch of life.

35.2.2.head: البَثّ
35.2.2.meaning: Grief so pressing that its bearer needs to give it utterance.

36.2.1.head: رُزء
36.2.1.meaning: A loss or bereavement that takes something precious from a person.

36.2.4.head: أَخضَع
36.2.4.meaning: Abject or bowed down in an appeal for pity.

37.1.1.head: قَعيدَك
37.1.1.meaning: A form of earnest adjuration, roughly “I beg you in God’s name.”

37.2.2.head: نَكَأَ
37.2.2.meaning: Pick open a partly healed wound.

38.1.1.head: قَصرَك
38.1.1.meaning: Enough, leave it there. A noun does the work of an imperative. The base gives a short vowel before the k. The reciter sustains it long enough to suggest a longer form.

38.2.1.head: كَفّ
38.2.1.meaning: My hand, singular. The single hand contrasts with the several men whose danger he witnessed.

38.2.3.head: المَنِيَّة
38.2.3.meaning: Death. The editions and the studio card give the singular. The sustained vowel can also sound like the plural, “deaths”.

39.1.6.head: غِبطَة
39.1.6.meaning: A happy condition others might wish to share.

40.1.6.head: مُتالِع
40.1.6.meaning: Mutali', a mountain associated by the commentators with the territory of Banu Amir.

40.2.4.meaning: Salma, one of the two mountains of Tayyi, here imagined as a massive support.

41.1.3.head: ظِئر
41.1.3.meaning: Foster-mothers, here three she-camels induced to nurse a single calf.

41.1.5.head: رائِم
41.1.5.meaning: Tenderly attached to the young, of nursing she-camels.

41.2.2.head: مَجَرّ
41.2.2.meaning: A drag mark left on the ground where the calf was pulled along.

41.2.4.head: حُوار
41.2.4.meaning: A young camel still dependent on its mother’s milk.

42.2.4.head: سَجَعَ
42.2.4.meaning: Answered a call in matching, repeated tones.

43.1.2.head: شارِف
43.1.2.meaning: An aged she-camel, singled out from the group.

43.2.4.head: البَرك
43.2.4.meaning: The whole company of camels kneeling on the ground.

44.1.1.head: أَوجَد
44.1.1.meaning: More deeply grieved. This completes the comparison begun with the three foster-camels.

45.1.4.head: المُحِلّ
45.1.4.meaning: Al-Muhill, a man of Yarbu identified in al-Yazidi’s account as the bearer of the news.

45.1.5.head: سَراة
45.1.5.meaning: The leading men of a people, to whom a complaint could be brought.

46.1.1.head: مَشمَتَة
46.1.1.meaning: Gloating over the disaster that befell another.

47.1.2.head: هِدم
47.1.2.meaning: A worn wrap or rag, still enough to cover a body.

47.1.4.head: سَوِيَّة
47.1.4.meaning: A pad or cloth on a camel’s back, also explained as a small riding saddle.

47.2.5.head: مُقَزَّع
47.2.5.meaning: A courier travelling light, freed of other burdens so that he can hurry.

49.2.5.head: أَجدَع
49.2.5.meaning: With the nose cut off, an image of lasting mutilation and disgrace.

50.2.5.head: مُمَزَّع
50.2.5.meaning: Torn apart, in pieces that would need to be gathered up.

51.2.3.head: شانِئ
51.2.3.meaning: His hater, from a word for personal enmity whose final hamza is eased here.
